title: Using Spacing to Enhance Diverse Forms of Learning: Review of Recent Research and Implications for Instruction https://pdf.retrievalpractice.org/spacing/Carpenter_etal_2012_EDPR.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 13, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises Carpenter and colleagues' research review on the spacing effect, which draws together evidence that distributing study sessions over time reliably beats massed cramming across ages and subjects, from word lists to mathematics to foreign language vocabulary. The review examines how the optimal gap between sessions depends on how long the material needs to be retained, with longer desired retention calling for longer spacing gaps. Barton pulls out concrete classroom tactics: brief weekly review of material from several weeks earlier, homework that re-exposes students to older content, cumulative exams and quizzes, and supplementing textbooks, which are usually organised in a non-distributed way, with interleaved sets of examples. He notes the review's reassuring conclusion that any spacing is likely to help, even if teachers can't hit the theoretically optimal gap, which lowers the barrier to actually implementing it.
points: The optimal spacing gap scales with how long retention needs to last — cramming produces fast but shallow mastery, while longer-term goals need longer gaps between sessions.
Cumulative exams and quizzes do double duty: they re-expose students to older material and give students a concrete reason to review it themselves.
Most textbooks present material in a non-distributed way, so teachers need to actively supplement lessons with content and examples from prior units.
Forgetting after several weeks doesn't mean the original teaching failed — re-exposure allows much faster relearning than teaching something entirely new.
quotes: This research review examines the spacing effect, demonstrating that distributed practice (spacing study sessions over time) significantly enhances long-term memory retention compared to massed practice (cramming).
They explore the optimal spacing intervals, finding that the ideal gap depends on the desired retention period, recommending longer gaps for longer-term retention.
Teachers can incorporate brief reviews of concepts learned several weeks earlier into each lesson.
Give cumulative exams and quizzes. This encourages students to review previously learned material.
Re-teach forgotten information. While students may forget information after several weeks, this does not mean that previous instruction was ineffective.

Instructors could give exams and quizzes that are cumulative. In addition to re-exposing students to information that they have previously learned, cumulative exams and quizzes provide students with a good reason to review information on their own
